vignette:
Kayla Morrison is a 25-year-old single woman who works as a city bus driver and was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that her supervisor described as "a change in her whole personality." Kayla served two years in the Army and was deployed to a forward operating base where, during her final month of service, she was riding in a convoy that struck an improvised explosive device. The vehicle lurched violently, filled with smoke and the sound of screaming, and Kayla lost consciousness briefly before coming to in a tilted cab, disoriented and unable to tell, in those first terrible seconds, whether she was still alive or whether the ringing in her ears and the spinning of the world around her meant she was dying. It was the dizziness - that nauseating, groundless vertigo - that she associated most viscerally with those seconds of not knowing. She was physically uninjured, but two of the soldiers with her were not, and she spent the next hour in conditions she describes only in fragments: dust, blood, the absence of any predictable order to what was happening around her.

Kayla left the military eight months ago and took the bus driving job believing, as she told her intake interviewer, that routine and structure would help her feel normal again. For a time it did. But the job that was supposed to anchor her has become one of its own sources of difficulty. Driving a bus means absorbing the unpredictability of the road - a car cutting in without warning, a passenger stumbling unexpectedly into the aisle, a sudden stop that sends her stomach dropping - and each of these moments, minor in isolation, land in Kayla's nervous system as something far more urgent. When something unpredictable happens during her route, her body responds before her mind can intervene: her heart hammers, her vision narrows, and most disturbingly, she feels dizzy - that same lightheaded, unmoored sensation from the cab of the vehicle, so that the trigger and the memory become briefly indistinguishable. These physical reactions arrive with such force that she has come to believe the dizziness itself is a warning signal, proof that something is about to go wrong, and this conviction sets her scanning - watching the mirrors obsessively, tracking every passenger who boards, reading every hesitation in traffic as a potential precursor to catastrophe.

The scanning and the hypervigilance have become constant features of her day. She cannot sit in the break room at the depot with her back to the door; she positions herself in the corner of every room so that she can see all entrances, and the physical tension this requires - the sustained readiness - exhausts her in ways she cannot fully explain to colleagues. What she can explain, and what she returns to repeatedly in session, is what she has come to believe about herself since the explosion. She had been, by her own account, someone defined by competence and physical confidence - a soldier, a driver, a person who handled things. She is now certain that version of herself is gone. She no longer feels capable of the things that once came easily, and this conviction - that she has been fundamentally diminished - colors every moment of her working day. When the threat monitoring intensifies, when she catches herself gripping the steering wheel and scanning the mirrors for the fifteenth time in a minute, it confirms for her what she already fears: that she is broken, that her life has been destroyed by what happened, that nothing she does behind the wheel or anywhere else carries any real meaning anymore.

This loop has tightened steadily over months. The belief that she is no longer capable makes ordinary stressors feel more threatening, which in turn makes her body more reactive, which produces the dizziness that throws her back into the worst moment of her life. She has started calling in sick on days when her roster includes unfamiliar routes. A supervisor meeting last month - during which she was told her performance reviews had slipped - was what finally brought her to seek help. What she is most afraid of is that the assessment will confirm what she already suspects: that the person she was before the convoy is simply not coming back.
